title: Interface Pollution and Package Boundaries in Go Microservices: Designing for Seam Clarity
description: How interface placement, method set design, and package topology determine testability, coupling, and operational cost in production Go backends.
linkedin_post:
Interface placement in Go is one of the highest-leverage design decisions you make in a large backend—and it's almost always done wrong the first time.

In a recent deep dive, I worked through the mechanics of why producer-side interfaces (defined in the package that implements them) create coupling that survives for years: wider method sets, heavier import graphs, and test doubles that break across packages when any method changes.

The production alternative:

→ Define interfaces in the consuming package, scoped to only the methods that consumer needs
→ Export concrete types from storage/adapter packages, not interfaces
→ Keep error types in the package that performs the operation—callers import the domain error, never the driver
→ Use generic types for data shapes (Page[T], Result[T]) but keep generic interfaces local to their consumer

The operational consequences of getting this wrong are concrete: a change to a shared interface file triggers recompilation across every dependent package, test doubles require framework support because they're too wide, and error handling collapses because raw driver errors leak across boundaries.

The test seam payoff alone justifies the discipline. A narrow consumer-side interface produces an 11-line hand-written stub. No reflection, no generated mocks, no framework. It compiles instantly and fails loudly when the interface changes.

I covered the full design mechanics—including how generics interact with package boundaries, how compilation blast radius maps to interface placement, and a concrete decision framework you can apply at every package boundary in a microservice.
